Mapping and interpolation

BAM models were produced to describe the distribution and abundance of breeding landbirds across boreal Canada for population size estimation. Models were produced using machine learning for 143 species using a modular approach, with separate models constructured for each bird conservation region. Predictions are provided at a spatial resolution of 1Km2, with regions blended together for wall-to-wall predictions across Canada.

Boosted regression tree

The model settings were chosen to yield complex response surfaces (an interaction depth of 3) because our goal is to accurately map the potential species' distribution in the region and our model is based on a large enough sample size for calibrating such complex response surfaces.
See Stralberg et al 2025 for modelling workflow (https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.70405).

Surveys were attributed to cells of a hexagonal grid (2.5 km diameter) and 1 survey per cell per year was randomly selected for each bootstrap.
Withheld data from each bootstrap were used for testing.

Predictor variables focussed on descriptions of vegetation structure, which are known to be strong predictors of bird distribution and abundance. Secondary predictor types included other known drivers of bird distribution and abundance including wetlands, anthropogenic disturbance, and climate variables, to maximize the spatial predictive capacity of the models.
Predictors were removed with step-wise variance inflation factor to a threshold of 10.
Predictors that explained less than 0.1% of deviance in the data were removed after model tuning.
